title: Producers II: batching, acks and idempotence
goal: By the end you can explain what happens between `send()` and the broker's answer, tune `linger.ms` and `batch.size` from metrics, read a `TimeoutException` correctly, and say what the idempotent producer prevents and what it doesn't.

warmup.q: A producer with default settings sends a payment, and the `Future` fails with a `TimeoutException` after `delivery.timeout.ms`. What do you know about the payment?
options: It was not written: the producer gave up before the broker stored it
It may or may not be in the log
It is in the log exactly once, because idempotence is on by default
It is in the log, but marked as failed so consumers skip it
warmup.why: The timeout means the producer stopped waiting, not that the broker never wrote the record. A request can be appended and its answer lost, or processed by a stalled broker after the producer gave up; the Try-it in this lesson shows four such payments. Idempotence prevents duplicates from the producer's own retries, but it can't tell you whether this record made it. Kafka has no "failed" marker on records.

sections.h: send() puts the record in a batch and returns
sections.body:
Your payment service emits 20,000 events a second at peak. If every `send()` became its own request and waited for its answer, two things would go wrong. A round trip to a broker in the same data centre takes about half a millisecond, so one thread waiting for each answer manages about 2,000 sends a second. And the broker would handle 20,000 requests a second, each with its own headers, checks and disk append, for records of a few hundred bytes. Most of its work would be overhead.

The producer avoids both with one design: `send()` doesn't send anything. It does three things on your thread and returns:

1. It serializes the key and the value into bytes.
2. It picks the partition (lesson 4 of this track).
3. It appends the record to a batch for that partition, in a buffer called the **record accumulator**, and returns a `Future<RecordMetadata>`.

A separate thread inside the producer, the **sender**, does the network work. It takes batches that are ready (the next section says when), groups them by the broker that leads their partition, and sends one produce request per broker carrying batches for many partitions at once. When the answer comes back, it completes each record's `Future` and runs its callback.

So the return of `send()` means "queued", not "written". You learn the outcome from the `Future` or the callback:

```java
producer.send(record, (metadata, e) -> {
    if (e != null) log.warn("payment {} not confirmed", id, e);   // runs on the sender thread
});
```

```kotlin
producer.send(record) { metadata, e ->
    if (e != null) log.warn("payment {} not confirmed", id, e)     // runs on the sender thread
}
```

Calling `send(record).get()` on every record throws the design away: your thread waits for each answer, and each batch carries one record. Use the callback, or keep the futures and check them later. `flush()` waits until everything queued so far has an answer, and `close()` does the same before it shuts down.

`send()` can still block, in two cases. The first send to a topic waits for its metadata, which says how many partitions it has and who leads them. And when the accumulator's memory, `buffer.memory` (32 MiB by default), is full because the brokers are slower than your code, `send()` waits for space. Both waits end after `max.block.ms`, one minute by default, with an exception. The producer is thread-safe, and the `KafkaProducer` javadoc says one instance shared by all threads is generally faster than several, because their records share batches.

sections.h: A batch leaves when it is full or when linger.ms runs out
sections.body:
The sender needs a rule for when a batch may leave. Sent too early, it carries one record. Held too long, every payment waits. Kafka uses two settings, per partition.

`batch.size` is the most a batch may hold: 16,384 bytes by default. When the next record doesn't fit, the batch is closed and may leave at once.

`linger.ms` is how long a batch may wait for more records: 5 ms by default. A batch that is 5 ms old may leave even if it holds one record. Until Kafka 4.0 the default was 0, meaning "send as soon as the sender is free". The producer docs give the reason: the efficiency of bigger batches usually makes latency similar or lower overall, despite the wait.

Put numbers on it. At 1,000 records a second for one partition, a record arrives every millisecond. With `linger.ms=5`, each batch collects about 5 records before it leaves. With 50, about 50, and each record waits up to 50 ms longer. A burst behaves differently: when 170 records of 100 bytes arrive at once, 163 fill a batch to 16 KB, and that batch leaves at once without waiting. Step through both below.

`linger.ms=0` doesn't mean one record per request either. The producer keeps up to 5 requests in flight per broker connection (`max.in.flight.requests.per.connection`). When they are all waiting for answers, new records pile up in the accumulator and leave together in the next request. So under heavy load batches form anyway; `linger.ms` matters most at moderate traffic, where the sender would otherwise send small batches as fast as it can.

Batches are also where compression happens. With `compression.type` set to `lz4`, `zstd`, `snappy` or `gzip`, the producer compresses each batch as one unit. The broker stores the compressed batch as it arrived (the topic's default `compression.type=producer` means "keep what the producer sent"), and the consumer decompresses it. Payment events repeat the same field names and currencies, so they compress well, and bigger batches compress better because there is more repetition to find. The Try-it measures all of this from the producer's own metrics.

frames.say: A closed batch may leave at once, so the full one goes out at t = 10 without waiting. The second batch is open and young, so it waits for its `linger.ms`: at t = 15 it leaves with 7 records. A batch leaves at whichever comes first, full or old enough.

try.title: Measure batching from the producer's own metrics
steps: From the `labs` folder, start the broker with `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml up -d --wait`, then create a one-partition topic: `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic ledger-events --partitions 1`.

Predict the records per request for `linger.ms` 0, 5 and 50 at about 1,000 records a second. Then run the demo (command below). It sends 500 payment events per setting and prints four producer metrics: `records-per-request-avg`, `batch-size-avg`, `compression-rate-avg` and `record-queue-time-avg`.
Keep the broker running for the next Try-its.

try.expect:
```text
linger.ms  compression  records/request  bytes/batch  compressed/raw  batch waited (ms)
        0  none                     1.3          170            1.00                0.5
        5  none                     4.8          457            1.00                5.5
       50  none                    38.5         3229            1.00               51.2
       50  lz4                     35.7          925            0.31               66.4
```
With `linger.ms=0` almost every record went alone, because the sender was free whenever a record arrived. 5 ms gave about 5 per request and 50 ms about 38, not 50, because `Thread.sleep(1)` takes a little over a millisecond on a laptop. The price is in the last column: each batch waited about `linger.ms` before it left. lz4 shrank each batch to under a third of its size. The bytes per batch include a header of about 60 bytes per batch, which is one more reason one-record batches waste space. Your timings will differ by a few milliseconds; the shape will not.

sections.h: Retries happen on their own, inside one deadline: delivery.timeout.ms
sections.body:
Lesson 3 of this track covered what the leader waits for before it answers. With `acks=all`, the default since Kafka 3.0, it waits until every in-sync replica has the batch. With `acks=1` it answers once its own copy has it. With `acks=0` the producer doesn't wait for any answer, so it never learns an offset (the metadata says -1) or an error.

Answers can be errors. Some are retriable: the condition may pass if the producer tries again. `NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER` (the leader moved), `NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS` (lesson 3's ISR floor) and a request that timed out are all retriable. Others are not: a record bigger than the broker allows, or a missing permission, fail the send at once.

For retriable errors the producer retries on its own. `retries` defaults to 2,147,483,647, in effect forever, with a pause between attempts that starts at 100 ms and doubles up to 1 second. Each attempt waits at most `request.timeout.ms`, 30 seconds by default, for its answer.

"Forever" is bounded by one setting: **`delivery.timeout.ms`**, 2 minutes by default. It starts when `send()` returns and covers everything after: the time in the batch, the wait for a free request slot, every attempt and every pause. When it runs out, the producer fails the record with a `TimeoutException`. The producer requires it to be at least `linger.ms` plus `request.timeout.ms`. The docs advise leaving `retries` alone and setting this deadline instead.

Now the part that matters most for payments. A `TimeoutException` tells you the producer gave up waiting. It doesn't tell you the record is missing. Picture the request that reached the broker, was appended, and whose answer was lost, or a broker that stalled with your request in its socket buffer and processed it after the producer had given up. The Try-it below does exactly that: it pauses the broker for 8 seconds while payments flow with a 5-second deadline. Five sends fail, and four of those five are in the log anyway.

So a failed send means **unknown**, not "not written". Code that treats it as "not written" and sends the payment again, or reports it as failed to the customer, gets it wrong some of the time. Retry it with the same idempotency key, and let the consumer drop the duplicate. Lesson 6 of this track builds that consumer.

try.title: Stall the broker past the deadline
steps: Open a second terminal in the `labs` folder and type, without pressing Enter: `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml pause kafka; sleep 8; docker compose -f env/kafka.yml unpause kafka`. `pause` freezes the broker's process without closing its connections.
In the first terminal, run the demo with a 5-second deadline (command below). It sends `pay-00` to `pay-29`, one every 500 ms. When `pay-10` appears, press Enter in the second terminal.

Read the failures and the last line. Then list the records written around the pause; use the offset of the last fast record before the failures (2015 in the run below): `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic ledger-events --partition 0 --offset 2015 --max-messages 8 --formatter-property print.offset=true`.

code.title: DeadlineDemo.java

alt.title: DeadlineDemo.kt
alt.src:
package sfz.kafka.l05.demo

import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.KafkaConsumer
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.KafkaProducer
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord
import org.apache.kafka.common.TopicPartition
import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer
import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
import java.time.Duration

/**
 * Sends one payment every 500 ms for 15 seconds to "ledger-events" and prints how long each took to be
 * acknowledged, or why it failed. Pause the broker for a few seconds while it runs.
 * Arguments: "idempotent" (the default) or "plain" (idempotence off), then delivery.timeout.ms (default 10000).
 */
fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    val idempotent = args.firstOrNull() != "plain"
    val deadlineMs = args.getOrNull(1)?.toInt() ?: 10_000
    val tp = TopicPartition("ledger-events", 0)
    val consumerConfig = mapOf<String, Any>(
        "bootstrap.servers" to "localhost:9092",
        "key.deserializer" to StringDeserializer::class.java,
        "value.deserializer" to StringDeserializer::class.java,
    )
    val start = KafkaConsumer<String, String>(consumerConfig).use { it.endOffsets(listOf(tp)).getValue(tp) } // this run starts here

    val config = mapOf<String, Any>(
        "bootstrap.servers" to "localhost:9092",
        "key.serializer" to StringSerializer::class.java,
        "value.serializer" to StringSerializer::class.java,
        "enable.idempotence" to idempotent,
        "request.timeout.ms" to 2_000,      // give up on one request after 2 s, then retry
        "delivery.timeout.ms" to deadlineMs, // give up on the record this long after send()
    )
    println("idempotence ${if (idempotent) "on" else "off"}, delivery.timeout.ms $deadlineMs, request.timeout.ms 2000")
    KafkaProducer<String, String>(config).use { producer ->
        repeat(30) { i ->
            val id = "pay-%02d".format(i)
            val sentAt = System.nanoTime()
            producer.send(ProducerRecord("ledger-events", "acct-1", id)) { md, e ->
                val ms = (System.nanoTime() - sentAt) / 1_000_000
                if (e == null) println("%s acked after %5d ms at offset %d".format(id, ms, md.offset()))
                else println("%s FAILED after %4d ms: %s".format(id, ms, e::class.simpleName))
            }
            Thread.sleep(500)
        }
    }

    // what did the log get?
    val written = mutableListOf<String>()
    KafkaConsumer<String, String>(consumerConfig).use { c ->
        c.assign(listOf(tp))
        c.seek(tp, start)
        val end = c.endOffsets(listOf(tp)).getValue(tp)
        while (c.position(tp) < end) c.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500)).forEach { written += it.value() }
    }
    val distinct = written.toSet().size
    println("the log got ${written.size} records for $distinct different payments: ${written.size - distinct} duplicates")
}

The consumer shows offsets 2017 to 2020 holding `pay-17` to `pay-20`, and `pay-22` at 2021. Five sends failed, yet four of them are in the log: their requests sat in the frozen broker's socket buffer and were appended when it woke, after the producer had given up. Only `pay-21`, still in the accumulator when its deadline passed, is missing. Offsets start at 2000 because `BatchingDemo` wrote 2,000 records; which payments fail depends on when you pressed Enter.

sections.h: Retries duplicate and reorder; the idempotent producer stops both
sections.body:
Retries create two problems of their own. The first is duplicates. If the leader appended a batch and the answer was lost, the retry is appended again, and the leader can't tell a retry from a new record. The second is reordering. With 5 requests in flight, request 1 can fail while requests 2 to 5 succeed. When request 1 is retried, its records land after the others. A capture overtakes its authorization within one partition, which breaks the one order lesson 4 promised.

The simplest fix for reordering is one request in flight at a time. That works, and it caps each broker connection at one round trip per batch. Kafka's fix keeps 5 in flight and fixes duplicates too: the **idempotent producer**, added in Kafka 0.11 and on by default since 3.0.

At start-up the producer gets a producer id from the broker. It numbers the records it sends to each partition 0, 1, 2 and so on, and every batch carries the producer id and the **sequence number** of its first record. For each producer the leader remembers the next sequence it expects and the last 5 batches it appended. Then:

- a batch with the next sequence is appended;
- a retry of one of the last 5 batches is a duplicate: the leader writes nothing and answers with the offset it gave the first time;
- anything else is a gap. The leader refuses it with `OUT_OF_ORDER_SEQUENCE_NUMBER`, and the producer resends the missing batch first.

That explains the three requirements: `acks=all`, `retries` above 0, and `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection` at most 5. Five is the number of batches the leader can recognise (`ProducerStateEntry.NUM_BATCHES_TO_RETAIN` in the broker). `acks=all` makes sure an acknowledged batch, with its producer id and sequence, is on every in-sync replica, so a new leader rebuilds the same state from its copy of the log.

The requirements have a trap. If you set a conflicting value, such as `acks=1` for speed, and don't mention `enable.idempotence`, the producer turns idempotence off silently. No warning, and duplicates and reordering are back. If you set `enable.idempotence=true` yourself, the same conflict is a `ConfigException` at start-up. So set it explicitly in every payment producer. The lab checks both behaviours on a real broker.

Know where the guarantee stops. It covers retries made by one producer instance, inside its delivery timeout. When your code catches a `TimeoutException` and calls `send()` again, that is a new record with a new sequence number, and it is written twice if the first one made it. A restarted service gets a new producer id. Duplicates across those boundaries are the consumer's problem, and lesson 6 of this track solves it with idempotency keys.

try.title: Duplicates with idempotence off, none with it on
steps: Run the demo with idempotence off and the default 10-second deadline: `./gradlew :kafka:demo -Pmain=sfz.kafka.l05.demo.DeadlineDemo -Pargs=plain` (Kotlin: `DeadlineDemoKt`). When `pay-10` appears, pause the broker for 5 seconds from the second terminal: `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml pause kafka; sleep 5; docker compose -f env/kafka.yml unpause kafka`.
Run it again with no arguments (idempotence on, the default) and pause the same way. Compare the offsets of the slow payments and the last lines.
Look at the last batches in the partition's segment file with the command below. Who wrote them, and with which sequence numbers? Scroll up for the batches of the `plain` run.
Stop the broker: `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml down -v`.

code.title: from the labs folder
code.src:
docker compose -f env/kafka.yml exec kafka bash -c \
  '/opt/kafka/bin/kafka-dump-log.sh --files /var/lib/kafka/data/ledger-events-0/00000000000000000000.log | grep baseOffset | tail -3'

try.expect:
Idempotence off (fast payments trimmed):
```text
pay-19 acked after  3558 ms at offset 2049
pay-18 acked after  4063 ms at offset 2050
pay-17 acked after  4568 ms at offset 2051
pay-16 acked after  5069 ms at offset 2052
pay-20 acked after  3054 ms at offset 2053
pay-21 acked after  2548 ms at offset 2054
the log got 34 records for 30 different payments: 4 duplicates
```
Idempotence on:
```text
pay-16 acked after  5036 ms at offset 2079
pay-17 acked after  4532 ms at offset 2080
...
pay-21 acked after  2521 ms at offset 2084
the log got 30 records for 30 different payments: 0 duplicates
```
The dump (fields trimmed):
```text
baseOffset: 2092 lastOffset: 2092 count: 1 baseSequence: 29 lastSequence: 29 producerId: 5 producerEpoch: 0 ...
```
Without idempotence, the frozen broker appended `pay-16` to `pay-19` at 2045 to 2048 when it woke, and then the retries appended them again at 2049 to 2052, in reverse order. Both failures from this lesson in one run: duplicates and reordering. With idempotence the retries were recognised as duplicates, every payment was written once and the offsets follow send order. The dump shows why: each batch carries the producer id and its sequence number, while the `plain` run's batches say `producerId: -1` and `baseSequence: -1`. Your counts depend on the timing of the pause.

refs.title: Kafka 4.4 design: the idempotent producer and delivery semantics

analogy: Think of the post room of a company. You drop a letter in the tray for its city and walk away: that's `send()` returning. A clerk empties each tray when the bag is full or when the van leaves every five minutes, whichever comes first: `batch.size` and `linger.ms`. Registered mail gets a receipt, and if the receipt doesn't come back, the clerk sends the letter again. With idempotence, every letter carries a sender number and a running number, and the receiving office throws away a second copy of a number it already has. The analogy breaks at the end: a letter the clerk gave up on may still be delivered, and the receiving office remembers only the last five bags from each sender.
in_your_world: In your Quarkus payment services, make three producer settings explicit: `enable.idempotence=true`, so a later change to `acks` fails at start-up instead of quietly allowing duplicates; `acks=all`; and a `delivery.timeout.ms` you chose, shorter than the Temporal activity timeout that wraps the send, so the activity sees the producer's answer before it gives up itself. Treat a failed send in that activity as "unknown": let Temporal retry the activity, send the same event with the same idempotency key, and make the consumer drop duplicates. Raise `linger.ms` to 10 or 20 ms and turn on `lz4` for high-volume event topics such as `ledger-entries`, and check `batch-size-avg` and `record-queue-time-avg` before and after.
mistake: Treating a `TimeoutException` from `send()` as "the payment was not sent" and sending it again under a new id, or telling the customer it failed. The exception only says the producer stopped waiting; the record may well be in the log, and the resend then charges or books it twice. People make this mistake because an exception usually means "nothing happened". The fix has two parts: the retry reuses the same idempotency key (not a new event id), and the consumer ignores a key it has already applied. The idempotent producer can't help here, because a second `send()` is a new record.

compare.title: A payments producer with its safety settings stated, in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java

kotlin.title: Kotlin
kotlin.src:
val producer = KafkaProducer<String, String>(
    mapOf(
        ProducerConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG to bootstrap,
        ProducerConfig.KEY_SERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG to StringSerializer::class.java,
        ProducerConfig.VALUE_SERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG to StringSerializer::class.java,
        ProducerConfig.ENABLE_IDEMPOTENCE_CONFIG to true,      // a conflicting setting now fails at start-up
        ProducerConfig.ACKS_CONFIG to "all",
        ProducerConfig.LINGER_MS_CONFIG to 10,
        ProducerConfig.COMPRESSION_TYPE_CONFIG to "lz4",
        ProducerConfig.DELIVERY_TIMEOUT_MS_CONFIG to 60_000,  // at least linger.ms + request.timeout.ms
    ),
)

producer.send(ProducerRecord("payments", accountId, eventJson)) { md, e ->
    outcome.complete(
        when (e) {
            null -> Outcome.WRITTEN
            is TimeoutException -> Outcome.UNKNOWN   // maybe written: retry with the same key
            else -> Outcome.FAILED
        },
    )
}

compare.note: Both pass a `Map` to the constructor; Java's `Map.of` takes up to ten pairs, which fits here. The callback's `e` is null on success. Kotlin's `when (e)` with `is TimeoutException` reads as one decision table, where Java needs an `instanceof` chain. `TimeoutException` here is `org.apache.kafka.common.errors.TimeoutException`, not the one in `java.util.concurrent`. The `outcome` future is yours: something like a `CompletableFuture<Outcome>` the calling code waits on.

worked.title: Choose linger.ms from your traffic, then check it

steps.say: `ledger-entries` takes 20,000 events a second at peak over 12 partitions, about 1,700 a second per partition, or one every 0.6 ms. Events are about 300 bytes. With the default `linger.ms=5`, a batch collects about 8 events, about 2.4 KB, far below `batch.size`. Filling 16 KB would take about 55 events, about 33 ms. The ledger consumer's latency budget is 200 ms, so `linger.ms=20` costs little: about 33 events, 10 KB, per batch.
Measure instead of trusting the arithmetic. Read the producer's own metrics after a few minutes of real traffic. `producer-metrics` is the group with the producer-wide averages.
Log the four numbers that describe batching: records per request, bytes per batch, compression ratio and how long batches waited.
steps.alt_code:
log.info("records/request {} bytes/batch {} compressed/raw {} waited {} ms",
    p.metric("records-per-request-avg"), p.metric("batch-size-avg"),
    p.metric("compression-rate-avg"), p.metric("record-queue-time-avg"))

steps.say: Read them. If `batch-size-avg` sits near 16,384, batches fill before `linger.ms` ends: raise `batch.size` (32 or 64 KB) before you touch `linger.ms`. If `record-queue-time-avg` is close to `linger.ms` and batches are small, traffic is light and the wait buys little: lower it. A `compression-rate-avg` of 0.3 means the network and the brokers' disks carry 30% of the raw bytes.

lab.title: Model the accumulator and the leader's duplicate check
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. 15 of 20 fail. The 5 that pass are in `ProducerOnBrokerTest` and need no code from you: they read a real producer's metrics and ask a Kafka 4.4 broker which producers it tracks (`Admin.describeProducers`). One of them proves that `acks=1` silently turns idempotence off.
In `BatchAccumulator.kt`, write `append`: use the partition's open batch if the record fits, otherwise close it and start a new one at `nowMs`; close a batch once it reaches `batchSize`.

Write `drain`: for each partition in order, take batches from the front while they are closed or at least `lingerMs` old. Run `BatchAccumulatorTest`; its trickle test reproduces the shape of the Try-it's table.

In `IdempotentLog.java`, write `append` in the order of its javadoc: a remembered batch is a `Duplicate`, the expected sequence is `Appended`, anything else is `OutOfOrder`. Keep at most `BATCHES_TO_RETAIN` remembered batches.
Run everything until all 20 pass. Then reread the test with five batches in flight and say why the leader may refuse batches that arrive early.
hints: In `append`, `queue.lastOrNull()?.takeIf { !it.closed }` is the open batch, if any. A record larger than `batchSize` goes into a fresh batch, which is then closed at once because it is already full.
`drain` must stop at the first batch of a partition that may not leave yet: a younger batch behind it can't overtake it.
Check for a duplicate before checking the sequence: a retry's base sequence is lower than the expected one, so the gap check would refuse it.

drill.title: Be the leader
drill.prompt: Producer 7's last five batches on this partition covered sequences 0 to 9 (two records each), so the leader expects 10 next. What does it answer to each of these, arriving in this order: (a) base sequence 10, 2 records; (b) base sequence 8, 2 records; (c) base sequence 14, 1 record; (d) base sequence 0, 2 records? Then write the decision as code in Java or Kotlin.

recap: `send()` serializes, picks the partition and appends to a batch in the accumulator, then returns a Future. A sender thread sends ready batches, one request per broker.
A batch leaves when it is full (`batch.size`, 16 KB) or old enough (`linger.ms`, 5 ms since Kafka 4.0). Compression works per batch, so bigger batches compress better.
Retriable errors are retried automatically until `delivery.timeout.ms` (2 minutes) runs out; then the send fails with a `TimeoutException`.
A failed send means unknown, not unwritten: the record may be in the log. Retry with the same idempotency key and dedupe at the consumer.
The idempotent producer (default since 3.0) tags batches with a producer id and sequence numbers; the leader drops retried duplicates and refuses gaps, so retries neither duplicate nor reorder.
Idempotence needs `acks=all`, `retries > 0` and at most 5 in-flight requests. A conflicting setting turns it off silently unless you set `enable.idempotence=true` yourself.

quiz.q: From lesson 3: `payments` has replication factor 3 and `min.insync.replicas=2`. Two followers drop out of the ISR for 40 seconds, then return. An idempotent producer with default settings sends during that time. What happens to its sends?
options: They fail at once with NotEnoughReplicasException
They are written to the leader alone and acknowledged
The producer retries the NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS errors; the sends succeed once the ISR is back, well inside the 2-minute delivery.timeout.ms
They are dropped silently because the ISR is too small
quiz.why: `NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS` is retriable, so the producer keeps retrying with backoff, and 40 seconds is inside the 2-minute `delivery.timeout.ms`. Once the followers rejoin the ISR, the next attempt is accepted. Only if the outage outlasted the deadline would the send fail, and then with a `TimeoutException`, not `NotEnoughReplicasException`. The second option is what `acks=1` would do.

quiz.q: To cut latency, a team sets `acks=1` on its payment producer and changes nothing else. What else changed?
options: Idempotence is now off, silently, so retries can duplicate and reorder records
Nothing else: idempotence stays on by default
The producer fails at start-up with a ConfigException
Retries are disabled
quiz.why: Idempotence requires `acks=all`. When you don't set `enable.idempotence` yourself, a conflicting setting turns it off without a warning; the lab's broker test shows the leader tracking no producer id afterwards. The ConfigException only happens when you also set `enable.idempotence=true` explicitly, which is why payment producers should.

quiz.q: A producer has `batch.size=16384` and `linger.ms=50`. A burst of 1,000 records of 100 bytes arrives within a millisecond, for one partition. What does the sender do?
options: Waits 50 ms, then sends all 1,000 records in one batch
Sends 1,000 one-record requests
Waits 50 ms, then sends 7 batches
Sends 6 full batches of 163 records at once; the last 22 records wait up to 50 ms
quiz.why: A batch can't exceed `batch.size`, so 163 records of 100 bytes fill one, and a full batch may leave without waiting for `linger.ms`. Only the last, partly filled batch lingers. The first option ignores `batch.size`, and `linger.ms` never delays a full batch.

quiz.q: Your code catches a `TimeoutException` from `send()` and calls `send()` again with the same payment. Idempotence is on. The first attempt was in fact written. What does the log hold?
options: One copy: the idempotent producer recognises the resend
Two copies: the second `send()` is a new record with a new sequence number
One copy: the broker compares the values and drops the second
No copy: the broker removes the first record when the producer times out
quiz.why: Idempotence covers the producer's own retries of one batch, which reuse its sequence number. A second `send()` call creates a new record with the next sequence number, so the leader appends it. The broker never compares values. That is why the consumer needs an idempotency key.

quiz.q: Your producer runs at 50 records a second per partition with `linger.ms=5`. You raise it to 100 to get bigger batches. What happens?
options: Batches grow to about 5 records, and every record waits up to 100 ms longer
Batches fill to `batch.size` and latency drops
Nothing changes, because linger.ms only applies under heavy load
Throughput doubles and latency stays the same
quiz.why: At 50 records a second, 100 ms collects about 5 records, a few kilobytes, nowhere near 16 KB. The batches are slightly bigger and each record waits up to 100 ms longer. `linger.ms` matters most at moderate traffic; here it buys little and costs latency.

flashcards.front: What does `send()` do before it returns?
flashcards.back: Serializes key and value, picks the partition, appends the record to that partition's batch in the accumulator, and returns a Future. The sender thread does the network work.

flashcards.front: When does a batch leave the accumulator?
flashcards.back: When it is full (`batch.size`, 16,384 bytes by default) or when it has waited `linger.ms` (5 ms by default since Kafka 4.0), whichever comes first.
The whole time from `send()` returning to the final answer: batching, waiting, every retry. 2 minutes by default; then the send fails with a TimeoutException.

flashcards.front: A send fails with a TimeoutException. Is the record in the log?
flashcards.back: Maybe. The producer stopped waiting; the broker may have written it. Treat it as unknown and retry with the same idempotency key.

flashcards.front: How does the leader spot a retried batch from an idempotent producer?
flashcards.back: By producer id and sequence numbers: it remembers the last 5 batches per producer and answers a repeat with the original offset, writing nothing.
A conflicting setting (`acks` other than all, `retries=0`, more than 5 in-flight requests) when `enable.idempotence` was not set explicitly.

flashcards.front: What doesn't the idempotent producer protect against?
flashcards.back: Your code calling `send()` twice, a restarted producer (new producer id), or anything beyond one partition. Those need idempotency keys or transactions.

terms.plain: The producer's buffer of batches, one queue per partition. `send()` appends to it; the sender thread drains it.
Records for one partition that travel and are stored together, and are compressed as one unit.
How long a batch may wait for more records before it leaves. 5 ms by default since Kafka 4.0.
The most bytes a batch may hold. A full batch leaves without waiting for `linger.ms`.
A broker error that may pass on its own, such as NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER; the producer retries it automatically.
The deadline for a record, from `send()` to the final answer, covering all retries. 2 minutes by default.
A producer whose retries can't duplicate or reorder records in a partition, thanks to a producer id and sequence numbers. On by default since Kafka 3.0.
The number an idempotent producer gives each record it sends to a partition: 0, 1, 2 and so on. Batches carry the number of their first record.

explain_back.prompt: A junior engineer asks: "We have idempotence on, so we can never get duplicate payments in Kafka, right?" Explain what idempotence does, how, and where it stops.
explain_back.answer: It stops one kind of duplicate. When the producer retries a batch because the answer got lost, the leader would normally append it again. With idempotence the producer has a producer id and numbers every record per partition, so the leader sees the same producer id and sequence on the retry, recognises it among the last five batches it remembers, writes nothing and returns the original offset. Gaps are refused too, so retries can't reorder records either. But it only covers that producer's internal retries. If our code gets a TimeoutException and calls send again, that is a new record with a new sequence number, and if the first one made it we have two. A restarted service also gets a new producer id. So we still put an idempotency key on every payment and the consumer skips keys it has already applied. And someone setting acks=1 without enable.idempotence=true would turn it off silently, so we set it explicitly.

deeper.body:
Look at the dump from the 5-second-deadline Try-it, if you kept the broker: the batches after the failures say `producerEpoch: 1` and their sequence numbers start again at 0. When a batch expires, the producer can't know whether the leader appended it, so its sequence numbers might now have a gap the leader would refuse forever. Since Kafka 2.5 (KIP-360) the idempotent producer handles this by bumping its **epoch**, a counter next to the producer id, and starting its sequences again at 0; the leader accepts sequence 0 from a newer epoch. Lesson 9 of this track uses the same epoch to fence a zombie transactional producer.

Two more settings change the picture. `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=1` keeps order without idempotence, at the cost of one round trip per batch to each broker; with idempotence there is no reason to lower it. The producer docs advise keeping `request.timeout.ms` (30 s by default) larger than the brokers' `replica.lag.time.max.ms` (also 30 s): with `acks=all`, a slow follower can hold an answer back for up to that long, and timing out earlier only adds retries and, without idempotence, duplicates. The Try-its used 2 s only to make the stall visible quickly.

Finally, `acks=0`. The producer sends and forgets: no answer, no offset (the metadata says -1), no retries that could help, and idempotence is off. It fits metrics or debug events you can afford to lose, never payments.
